objects.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage
objects.purpose: Decelerated the Eagle to a gentle lunar landing and served as the launch platform for crew ascent.
objects.story: Remained at Tranquility Base after Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin blasted off in the ascent stage. It has stood silently on the lunar surface since July 1969, bearing the historic plaque proclaiming 'We came in peace for all mankind'.
objects.science: Carried the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP) including the Passive Seismic Experiment and the Laser Ranging Retroreflector, which provided precise Earth-Moon distance measurements for decades.

objects.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
objects.purpose: Transported astronauts and scientific equipment across the Hadley-Apennine region to expand surface exploration radius.
objects.story: Parked by Commander David Scott at the 'VIP site' approximately 160 meters from the Lunar Module Falcon so its television camera could record the first live broadcast of an Apollo lunar liftoff. It remains parked in Hadley-Apennine today.
objects.science: Expanded lunar exploration traverses to 27.9 kilometers, enabling the recovery of the ancient 4.1-billion-year-old 'Genesis Rock' (anorthosite sample 15415) and proving off-world wheeled transportation systems.

objects.name: Perseverance Parachute and Backshell
objects.purpose: Slowed the rover capsule through supersonic entry and protected the vehicle during atmospheric descent.
objects.story: Jettisoned at 2.1 km altitude during entry, descent, and landing in Jezero Crater. The backshell and parachute impacted at high speed, creating a debris field that was later surveyed and photographed from the air by the Ingenuity helicopter during Flight 26.
objects.science: Provided rare high-resolution aerial imagery of landing hardware wreckage on another planet, validating parachute canopy aerodynamics, suspension line integrity, and backshell structural crush performance for future Mars Sample Return missions.

objects.name: Curiosity Sky Crane Descent Stage
objects.purpose: Lowered the 900-kilogram Curiosity rover to the surface of Gale Crater using throttleable rocket engines and tethers.
objects.story: After successfully placing Curiosity onto the surface, the tethers were cut and the powered descent stage executed an intentional flyaway maneuver, crash-landing approximately 650 meters away to avoid damaging the rover with rocket exhaust and debris.
objects.science: Validated the revolutionary Sky Crane landing architecture for heavy planetary rovers. Its impact scar and blast plumes were cataloged by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE camera to study Martian soil disturbance and high-velocity cratering mechanics.
objects.imageCredit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / Univ. of Arizona (HiRISE ESP_028269_1755 / PIA16001)

objects.name: Surveyor 3 Soft Lander
objects.purpose: Demonstrated uncrewed lunar soft landing and sampled lunar soil with a surface scoop before the Apollo landings.
objects.story: Landed in Oceanus Procellarum in April 1967. In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed nearby and walked to the probe, inspecting it and recovering its TV camera and mechanical scoop to return to Earth.
objects.science: Became the only robotic probe visited on another celestial body by astronauts. Analysis of returned parts gave humanity the first empirical data on how long-term exposure to solar radiation, vacuum, and micrometeoroids degrades aerospace materials.

objects.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
objects.purpose: Demonstrated powered, controlled atmospheric flight in Mars's ultra-thin atmosphere.
objects.story: Completed 72 successful flights over three years before sustaining rotor damage in January 2024 at Neruda Crater. Reprogrammed to act as a permanent stationary surface weather station, transmitting telemetry to the Perseverance rover.
objects.science: Proved aerodynamic rotorcraft flight on another world across 17 kilometers of Martian terrain, providing aerial scouting for Perseverance and establishing the foundation for future aerial planetary exploration missions.
